content: The American sycamore, scientifically known as Platanus occidentalis, is a tree species native to North America. It is also referred to as the American plane, Occidental plane, or Buttonwood. In North America, it is commonly called sycamore, though this name can also apply to other tree species. The American sycamore is easily identified by its distinctive bark, which exfoliates in large, irregular patches. This shedding process reveals a mottled surface of greenish-white, gray, and brown hues. The smaller branches often appear as though they have been whitewashed. This characteristic is due to the rigid structure of the bark, which lacks the elasticity to expand as the tree grows. Consequently, the bark peels off to accommodate the growth of the underlying wood. This species is a massive tree, typically reaching heights of 30 to 40 meters (98 to 131 feet) and trunk diameters of 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6.5 feet) in optimal conditions. Exceptional specimens have been recorded at 51 meters (167 feet) in height and nearly 4 meters (13 feet) in diameter. Historical accounts suggest some trees exceeded 5 meters (16 feet) in diameter, though these reports are difficult to verify. The tree often divides into multiple secondary trunks near the ground, with spreading limbs forming an irregular, open canopy. The roots are fibrous, and the trunks of older, larger trees are frequently hollow. A unique feature of the sycamore is the way its leaves protect the developing buds. Unlike most trees, where buds are visible in the leaf axils during late summer, the sycamore's buds are enclosed within an enlarged base of the petiole, forming a tight protective case. Bark The bark of the American sycamore is dark reddish-brown at the base, breaking into oblong, plate-like scales. Higher up the tree, the bark becomes smoother and lighter in color, often pale gray. It peels off in thin plates, exposing a surface that can appear pale yellow, white, or greenish. Wood The wood of the sycamore is light brown with a reddish tint. It is heavy, weak, and difficult to split. It is commonly used for furniture, interior house finishes, and butcher's blocks. The specific gravity of the wood is approximately 0.5678, and its weight is about 35 to 39 pounds per cubic foot. Winter Buds The winter buds are large, conical, and three-scaled. They form during the summer within the petiole of the fully grown leaf. The inner scales of the buds enlarge as the shoot grows. Notably, the sycamore lacks a terminal bud. Leaves The leaves are alternate, palmately veined, and broadly ovate or orbicular in shape. The leaves are threeto five-lobed, with broad, shallow sinuses and acuminate lobes that may be toothed, entire, or undulate. When emerging from the bud, the leaves are pale green and covered with a fine, pale tomentum. Fully grown leaves are bright yellow-green on the upper surface and paler beneath. In autumn, the leaves turn brown and wither before falling. The petioles are long and abruptly enlarged at the base, enclosing the buds. Stipules with toothed borders are conspicuous on young shoots but are caducous. Flowers The sycamore flowers in May, coinciding with leaf emergence. The tree is monoecious, producing separate male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers on the same tree. The staminate flowers are dark red and borne on axillary peduncles, while the pistillate flowers are light green with red tinges and borne on longer terminal peduncles. The calyx of the staminate flowers consists of three to six small, scale-like sepals, which are slightly united at the base. The pistillate flowers have three to six rounded sepals, shorter than the acute petals. The stamens in the male flowers are as numerous as the calyx divisions, with short filaments and elongated, two-celled anthers. The pistil of the female flowers has a superior, one-celled ovary surrounded by long, jointed, pale hairs. The styles are long, incurved, and red, with stigmatic surfaces. Fruit The fruit consists of brown, spherical heads about an inch in diameter, hanging on slender stems 3 to 6 inches long. These fruit heads persist through the winter and are composed of numerous achenes, each approximately two-thirds of an inch in length. Distribution The American sycamore is commonly found in riparian and wetland areas within its native range, which extends from Iowa to Ontario and Maine in the north, Nebraska in the west, and southward to Texas and Florida. Closely related species are found in Mexico and the southwestern United States. The tree has been cultivated for timber and has become naturalized in some areas outside its native range. It grows well in regions such as Bismarck, North Dakota, and as far south as Okeechobee, Florida. The American sycamore is also well-suited to the Australian climate and is widespread in the cooler southern states, including Victoria and New South Wales. Cultivation The sycamore is highly tolerant of urban environments and is frequently planted as a shade tree. It transplants well and grows rapidly. Propagation and Pests The sycamore leaf beetle is a common pest that feeds on the American sycamore. Diseases The American sycamore is susceptible to plane anthracnose disease (Apiognomonia veneta, syn. Gnomonia platani), a fungal infection introduced from the Oriental plane (Platanus orientalis), which has developed significant resistance to the disease. While the disease rarely causes severe harm or death, it often results in partial defoliation, making the tree less visually appealing. The disease manifests as small black spots near the veins of newly expanded leaves, causing them to turn brown, shrivel, and fall prematurely. By early July, affected trees often produce a second set of leaves while the first set remains brown and unsightly on the branches. This shortens the tree's effective growing season. Due to its susceptibility, the American sycamore is less commonly planted, with the more resistant London plane (Platanus × hispanica, a hybrid of P. occidentalis and P. orientalis) being preferred. History The Buttonwood Agreement, which established the New York Stock Exchange, was signed under a Buttonwood tree, another name for the American sycamore. During the Cretaceous and Tertiary periods, sycamores were abundant in the forests of Greenland and Arctic America. They also once thrived in central Europe, where they have since disappeared.
